title: Rhythm, syncopation and imitators of the Dixieland band
summary: He says he changed the rhythm in Chicago, defends his band's unison style against one-chorus imitators, and argues early Black bands only played scored ragtime. He also describes faking tunes, Reisenweber's pay, rival bands and Marshall Stearns.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: You don't see anything in front of me that I take notes from, only just from what comes to my mind. That's why I don't have it in chronological order. I can only tell you what I can think of at the time. Maybe my talk may be gobbled up a little bit, that I might put this one before the other one, the other one before the other one. But I am telling you the true facts of this music. It was in Chicago where I changed the rhythm. They had a certain dance team. They were doing a castle walk. And up in the north, people were doing a different step than they were doing a two-step in New Orleans. Here they did a skip step, which is called a two-step. Over there they did more like a walking step. After the first two numbers I played, maybe you won't believe that I was a good dancer. Maybe nobody vouched for that either because many of the men of my age that would know about me are dead. But I can tell you that nobody could beat me dancing. I don't give a darn. Whether they come from New York, Chicago, Paris, anywhere else on a dance floor. But with a rehearse dance they may be. But I say if I grabbed any individual girl that I danced better with her, then them professionals could. Because I had a way of making them follow the way I'd want them to go. In other words, a strong lead. Getting back to this rhythm, I noticed that they made a walk step. I said, we ain't going to go here, to myself. I told the drummer, I said, look, let's play this march. Slow it down. And we played a march like I played in street parades in New Orleans. And we slowed it down. From then on. Then we played other numbers in the same rhythm, syncopation, which was a different syncopation than the ragtime. Ragtime was jumping syncopation. Here again they'll dispute me. It says syncopation is all alike. But I say it is not. Because you could write syncopation of ragtime and you couldn't write these syncopated jazz names that we made. There would have to be a choir listening to a recording. Now each time a man listened to that record and he made this lick, he naturally would try to capture the way we played it. But not being one of us, it would come out his way. It would be a little different. But to me, I could feel that was what he was trying to play. One man on top of the other, they start putting these licks together. One, then two, then three, then four. They even included the endings of our tune. There's a lick. That's the ending. And they start and so on and down until they had them all together. But many people say, well why did I do that? Well my limited knowledge of music at that time, which is probably the same, I don't think I've progressed much more, yet I've heard them play, and I wouldn't still put them that way again because to me melody is music. Not a lot of noise and rhythm or background which you can play against supposed melody. It wouldn't be music. Because if you played one tune with the same background, you played the other one, they were the same. You must define that thing as melody. That was the reason why when I went to England, that's a foreign country. A lot of these guys said they went before us, they were too soon. The people didn't understand their music. They didn't have what it took to make them understand. Because if they had, they would have been known. And I never have been known in this world. I'd been still here with a pair of pliers, pulling on electric wires and connecting electric wires up like I used to do in my youth. But it looked like God put us together. And we were the only five that played this type of music. And I have never heard of a band. They have tried to imitate us, tried to play the way we played, but they never could play in unison. They took this stuff and played chorus by chorus. One man playing one chorus, one playing another. But they embodied the licks of the Dixieland Jazz band. And they played the licks of the chorus. So I never called that anything at all because any man plays one chorus in a tune and actually when he got to the end of the tune he was strong. If any cornet player is listening to me he'll know what I mean. But if he's not a cornet player he wouldn't understand me. Because when you knock off and you carry the ball and you pull it, you drive it all the way. You don't have time to run sidetrack or jump a curve or go this way or that way like these fellas have. They made it easy for themselves. In other words I'd call them one chorus men. They don't play the way we play. They play some of the idioms. They've contracted them, they've made them larger, yes. But they haven't improved any of them. And the rhythm they use, as long as they use it, that's Dixieland rhythm. And no one else will tell me it's different until they change that rhythm. Now, then I say they're playing different American music. That is what's embodied in American music. It's the recordings of the Dixieland jazz band. The writers have always said this rhythm came from Africa. Yet when it was brought to Africa these Negroes didn't know anything about it. They liked it, but they never knew nothing about it. It was tried on them. Now 40 years have passed, almost going on to 50 years. These Negroes are being civilized. They live in big towns, they work in big towns. They may have come in contact with this music since then. I don't say colored men can't play music because in 40 years they have did a lot of advancing in their music. But you've got to run to the facts as this. I'm talking about the early Negroes. They couldn't play a dance, nothing. They couldn't play nothing. And I mean what I say. Outside of a few bands that read music, many of them were taught by white men how to read that music and play. And they played the same ragtime as they played in the North because it was all scored music. That's P. Ron, Robichaud, and this fellow played a cornerhead of brass band, Manuel Perez. Now they played conventional music. I could show you on a record here a white man playing Too Much Mustard, Prince's Band. And I'd show you Jim Europe who was a colored man playing. And they both have the same rhythm. It's the same tune as written. They're playing for music. They had fake bands in my days, plenty of them. And every band, I'm going way back now because I think this is very interesting. And every band, the cornerhead player, carried a melody and he was the leader. Now you hear men today playing a bass or drums telling you what they played. They ain't played nothing. Because what they played was nothing but accompaniment. The man who played that harp styled that band. If he was a clarinet and he carried a melody, he was styling the band. Because when he hit his two licks with his foot down, and he gave the notes that he was the player what tune he was to play, or he either told them what number he was going to play, and if it was a strange band he'd tell them the key he was going to play in. So they'd know. And he'd hit the two licks and they all hit simultaneously, go together. Now many bands were all carnet bands. They didn't know harmony. Many of them used to play bass on the trombone, what they called a vamp style. Vamp style is nothing but boop, boop, boop, boop, bass. Why they did that? Because they didn't know how to put the trombone. Just like when I put the rooster crow in there, I didn't know what the hell to put in there. So I was a fake and I went, eeeeee. I didn't know what to put in there. I wasn't educated in music that I could pick up a rhyme out of some book somewhere and slip it in there like the men today can do. They can go to work and what they'll learn is exercises. If they hit a chord, they know what the chord is. They'll run an exercise or something and put it in their own way. But I didn't have that. I didn't have that knowledge. And that's why all this humbug came up. The flutter tongue come in when I used to hear these guys triple tongue. Is that flutter tongue? No, that's just a common man trying to cover up like a cat would do his dirt. I didn't know any better. And that's why that come about. Later, the good musicians use it today. It's high class today. It's not low class. In my time they used to throw rocks, potatoes, and anything they could get at me. And the men of the boys that are talking today used to come where I used to play with these string bands and throw at the house where I was playing because they thought I was lousy. Because what I played was different than they played. I was thrown on my own to compose my tunes. I told you how I composed several other tunes. And most of the tunes that I have ever composed came that way. I used to go to a show, listen to the tune. Come back that night I couldn't play it. That night laying in bed this tune would come to me. Some of it anyway. The next day I'd come on the job I'd say to Regis, I'd say, run this over. I'd get the chords on the piano. I'd say run this over. I think I've got the melody on this tunes we went to last night. And the people would ask for me advice and weapons I didn't know. So if I knew the first four or five bars in the chord construction, that's all I wanted. And when I played them, they were not like the tune that I had to wait. Maybe the four or five bars that I could commit to memory was mostly exactly the same. But I'll bet you the rest wasn't because I didn't know the melody and I'd fake it. I'd put different licks and different other things in there to fit the chord construction. Those people went wild. They thought that was the greatest thing that ever happened. They never heard music played like that before. How could they hear music? Because whenever they went there they would have men played by music. They didn't hear no impromptu or improvisation on any tune. Speaking of rising weathers I played there 112 weeks consecutively. And we never made less than $250 and we made as high as $300 a week counting our collections. There's nobody that ever lived that ever played that much. Besides we played all the theaters around New York in conjunction with rising members. Outside of that sign we were billed as the creators of jazz. And that's where we were taking that point from that on. And in the contract you'll find that we played exclusive music. That we were playing with the other songs. And you'll see in paragraphs one of us had dropped out the band. They could sue the rest of us for damages that's being done because our rhythm was different than any other band that ever had to foreplayed or ever played. And rising weathers tried out many bands to try to get their expenses down. I had told you about these negros coming up to New York. They played for Gloria Goodwin and this fellow Webb. I always get Jack Webb but it ain't Jack Webb. It's another Webb. They did a dancing act for this Dolodrina at the Moomont. They stayed almost two weeks. They went into Vaudeville. And when they write about them they say they had an extended engagement. Let me tell you the extended engagement they had. They extended them out the back door. That's the extended engagement they had. And the item, and I mean the variety, I've already mentioned that again, I'm going to tell you again. You read it March the 10th, that every band on Broadway that played or supposed to play jazz was classed as imitators. I have never kept anybody from getting a job on Broadway. In fact, I sent for boys. I helped them out to get jobs. Many of them I got out of jail for no visible means of support. We put them on there and paid their way back to New Orleans so they could go back and work. Would it be good taste for me to mention some of them guys? Sure, go right ahead, huh? Well, I'll tell you one was Eddie Rowland. He came up there with Tom Brown's reorganized band. And after Tom Brown and them went back, I don't know where they went to New Orleans or Chicago, I had given money to several of their members, fair, because they couldn't get a job. They tried out at Healy's. This is in the early part of the jazz business. They played there one night and they never let them finish the night. They let them go. Their music was no different than other music that was being played around. They found no difference in them because they never made a hit and they didn't get the job. They tried out at Rice and Weathers. And their agent told them you could put these men behind a crate and you wouldn't know the difference between these boys and the original Dixieland jazz band. Well, I lived around the corner at the Punchet Train Hotel it was called, man. And I came by and as I came by the bartender said, give me a notice to come on in. He said, go upstairs and listen. He said, some guys are trying to get you down. I went and I stayed in the lobby and I heard them play a number. And they tried to play some numbers that belonged to me. Mr. Wagner and Mr. Schultz, the manager, walked out on them while they were playing the first number. That's where Tom Brown says he played at Rice and Weathers. He tried out at Rice and Weathers but he didn't have a job there. That I had positive because I was there for three years. And no other band played there but our band. Now, they come to New Orleans and they tell different stories. I'll tell you how the stories thought. I had began to tell you about Marshall Stein's story. How he started up all this to put the Negros in. Well, this man comes from Columbia University where most of them all taught pro-criminalists and Negro integration. Most of the only guys that come out there, you'll find them in LSU and many other places. They were learned at Columbia University. That's the heartbeat. Marshall Stein's right now holds a position up there. He came down to New Orleans and he sold them a bill of goods to Myra Menville and Dr. Sushant. He said, well, they may be intelligent people. They may be smarter than I am because they have set up what you call a racket to form a jazz club to disseminate or put liars out in the public. Untruths, all written by Negroes who did nothing or created nothing in this music in the days and God knows where they played. But their word is more truth than mine who have made history and has the proof to back up this historical part that the original Dixieland jazz band made. I'd like to read your letter. I'll let you read it but the way you put all these dots and dashes in there, if you'll eliminate them dots and dashes. I'll let him read it. I'd like you to read this here. This was for the celebration of the introduction of jazz into England in 1990 by the one and only original Dixieland jazz band led by Nick LaRocca. This article appeared in the States paper in regards to me having an invitation to go to England for the commemoration of this affair. Would you kindly take your time and read down? This is Miss Bendel's letter. This is LaValle.
